failure_patterns.pattern: rule_ignored: The answer was a related setting, example, or candidate rather than the target specified by the clue or its full set of details.

rejected_edits.content: Before choosing a candidate, use the clue's head nouns, pronouns, and demonstratives to identify the kind of answer requested: a manner, place, role, institution, species, person, or other category. Phrases such as “this play” or “this vitamin” point to the work or substance itself, not its setting or an example. When wording such as “one of these [plural class]” appears, distinguish the class from an individual member and return the entity the clue's grammar actually requests. Return the target, not a consequence or associated entity used to identify it.
rejected_edits.target: Before choosing a candidate, use the clue's head nouns and pronouns to identify the kind of answer requested: a manner, place, role, institution, species, person, or other category. Return that target, not a consequence, associated entity, or example used to identify it.

rejected_edits.content: For fragmentary quotes, titles, nicknames, or familiar sayings and proverbs, infer the omitted word or phrase that completes the clue rather than echoing the supplied text. When an ellipsis marks an unfinished phrase, treat it as a fill-in-the-blank and prefer the missing wording over attribution to a related work or performer that happens to be prominent in context.
rejected_edits.target: For fragmentary quotes, titles, nicknames, or familiar sayings and proverbs, infer the omitted word or phrase that completes the clue rather than echoing the supplied text.

rejected_edits.content: Use the context-supported conventional identifying form: include the full name when it is needed or is the canonical form for identifying the entity; use a shorter form only when it is conventionally used and unambiguous.
rejected_edits.target: Use a name form that uniquely identifies the entity: give the complete identifying name when needed, but a surname or shorter form is appropriate when it is unambiguous.
